place: A mixed forest clearing beside a shallow pond, at the edge between grass and treeline, as summer turns to autumn and then winter.
outcome: Over several weeks the days shorten and nights grow cold; leaves change color and drop, grass stops growing and browns, the pond skins with ice on the coldest nights and eventually freezes solid at the edges, and the geese fly off while the hedgehog shelters under the fallen leaves. A person returning after this finds a stiff, quiet, white-rimmed clearing instead of the green one they left, and the pond can bear weight in places but not in the open middle.

place: A river bend cutting through soft clay banks below a stand of willows, over a wet season of heavy rain.
outcome: Heavy rain over several weeks swells the river, and the current cuts into the soft clay bank on the outer bend, undermining a willow's roots until it leans, while sediment drops on the inner bend and builds a new gravel bar. By the end of the wet season the river's main flow has shifted a few strides sideways, leaving a shallow stagnant channel where the old course was, and the willow now stands with its roots partly bare in standing water.

place: A dry gully at the edge of open grassland, where a deer died of an old injury.
outcome: Within a day, crows find the carcass by sight and smell and tear at the softest parts; a fox follows the crows in and takes the rest of the meat over the next couple of nights, dragging a leg off. Flies lay eggs in the exposed flesh within hours, and by the third day maggots are working through what is left; after a week or more only hide, sinew and bones remain, scattered and picked clean, with flattened grass and a patch of dark, enriched soil where the fluids soaked in.

place: A wooden post-and-rail fence around a goat pasture, standing in damp ground near a stream, over a rainy autumn.
outcome: Weeks of rain keep the lower rail and the base of one post constantly wet, and the wood there softens and rots while the rest of the fence stays sound. The weakened rail gives way when a goat leans on it to reach fresh grass on the other side, and the gap widens as more goats push through; the goats wander into a neighbor's garden and strip the vegetables before anyone notices, and one wanders further and is not found again for a day.

place: A village's shared well, dug beside the main square, after a dead rat falls in during a dry spell.
outcome: A rat that fell in and drowned goes unnoticed for days because the well is deep and dark; the water starts to smell and taste foul as the body breaks down in it, and the first people to draw from it after that get bad stomachs. Word spreads through the village within a day or two, and people stop drawing from the well and start walking to the stream outside the walls instead, a longer and more exposed trip, until someone eventually hauls the rat out and the well is left unused for a while before anyone trusts it again.

place: A footpath through a stand of tall pines on a slope, during a night of strong wind.
outcome: A night of strong, gusting wind puts more sideways force on a tall pine than its roots can hold in the loose slope soil, and it topples across the footpath, tearing a slab of earth and roots up with it and leaving a bare pit behind. The fallen trunk blocks the path completely; over the following weeks rain softens the bark, moss grows on the shaded underside, and a few opportunistic saplings sprout in the new gap of sunlight the fall opened in the canopy, so someone walking the path later finds it blocked and has to go around through the trees.

place: A stretch of dry grassland and scrub at the end of a rainless summer, during a thunderstorm with little rain.
outcome: Lightning strikes a dead, dry tree standing alone in the grass and sets its brittle wood alight; the fire drops burning fragments into the tinder-dry grass around its base and spreads outward with the wind, faster through grass than through the damper scrub at the field's edge. It burns through the night until the same storm finally brings heavy rain that douses what is left, leaving a blackened, smoking scar of bare ground and charred stumps where grass and scrub used to stand.

place: A timber grain store raised on posts at the edge of a farmstead, over the weeks after harvest.
outcome: Mice find a gap at the base of the grain store soon after it is filled and move in, breeding quickly on a steady food supply with no predators reaching them. Over a few weeks they gnaw through sacking, spoil far more grain than they eat with droppings and urine, and their numbers climb; a cat drawn by the smell and the noise starts hunting around the store, picking off mice night by night, and within another couple of weeks the population has dropped sharply, though the grain already spoiled stays spoiled.

place: A muddy creek bank where the only water available is cloudy with silt, no clean spring nearby.
lines: strain the muddy water through my shirt into the waterskin
pour the water through my shirt again
outcome: Stretching the shirt's woven fabric over the waterskin's mouth and pouring the muddy water through it catches the larger silt and grit in the weave, so what drips through is noticeably clearer, though still faintly cloudy since the weave is coarser than the finest particles. Pouring it through a second time, especially once the shirt already holds a layer of trapped silt, clears it further but slows the flow, and the shirt itself ends up muddy and needs washing before it can be worn again; the water is clearer, not purified, and could still carry anything the creek does that a weave cannot stop.

state_after: water: visibly clearer but not fully clear, untested for anything dissolved

waterskin: partly filled
stress: a fabric's mesh property (weave gap size) doing filtering work it was never designed for, with an honest limit (dissolved matter passes regardless)
temptation: a special rule 'shirts purify water' instead of deriving partial filtering from weave gap size versus particle size, with dissolved contaminants explicitly untouched

place: A steep snow-covered hillside above a frozen valley, after a heavy snowfall.
lines: sit in the shield and push off down the slope
outcome: The shield's broad, curved, smooth-faced underside presents a low-friction surface against packed snow, so sitting in its bowl and pushing off lets the player slide downhill under gravity much like a sled would, picking up real speed on the steeper stretch. The shield's rim, meant to deflect blows rather than steer, gives little control over direction, so a shift in the slope's angle sends the ride off-line, and it clips the rock outcrop partway down hard enough to crack the wood and pitch the player off into the snow rather than stopping cleanly.

place: A narrow lane between two crumbling stone walls, where loose mortar and small stones sometimes fall from above.
lines: put the cooking pot on my head before going under the wall
outcome: The pot's rigid iron shell and rounded shape sit over the skull with an air gap between metal and scalp, so when a fist-sized stone drops from the wall and strikes it, the hard shell spreads and absorbs the blow rather than letting it hit bone directly, saving the player from a real injury, though the impact rings loudly enough to daze and half-deafen them for a moment and the pot itself takes a visible dent. The pot's lack of a strap means it sits loose and nearly slides off with the impact, and it is now dented enough that food cooked in it afterward sits unevenly.

place: A hunting camp with a torn leather pack and a fresh kill nearby, no metal needle to hand.
lines: sharpen a splinter of bone into a point
use the bone point to sew the torn pack with sinew
outcome: Splitting a long bone and grinding one end against the whetstone produces a thin, rigid, sharp-tipped sliver that can pierce leather the way a needle does, since what a needle needs is hardness and a fine point, not any particular material. Working the sinew through the holes it pierces closes the tear, though the bone point is brittle compared to metal and has no eye, so the player has to push it through then thread the sinew behind it by hand each stitch, which is slow, and the tip chips slightly after enough punctures through the tougher, thicker part of the leather.

place: A hearth-side camp after a big fire, with a greasy pot and no proper soap on hand.
lines: mix the cold ash with water and rub it on the pot

outcome: Wood ash mixed with water releases the alkaline compounds left over from burning, and rubbed against grease that alkaline paste breaks the grease's grip on the metal the way soap does, since soap itself is made from ash and fat cooked together, and grinds off caked residue by simple abrasion as well. The pot comes cleaner than plain water would leave it, though the ash paste is gritty and mild rather than a true soap, so heavier grease needs real scrubbing and some film remains, and it leaves the player's hands dry and a little irritated from the alkalinity.

temptation: a rule 'ash cleans pots' instead of deriving cleaning from alkalinity and abrasiveness, and the hand irritation from the same alkalinity

place: A flooded stretch of river valley after days of heavy rain, where the water is too deep and fast to wade, with a fallen barn door lying nearby.
lines: lay the barn door flat on the water and push it out

outcome: The door's flat, wide, air-filled wood displaces enough water to float the player's weight, working as a crude raft the same way any broad slab of wood less dense than water would. Lying flat and paddling by hand moves it slowly across the slack water near the bank, but out in the main current the water's push overpowers the little steering hand-paddling gives, so the door drifts downstream faster than it crosses and the player lands well below where they aimed; the iron hinges, being denser than wood, drag one corner down and tip the door enough to nearly pitch the player off partway across.

place: A workshop bench with a wooden chest whose lid is held by a single slotted screw, no proper tool at hand.
lines: fit the edge of the coin into the screw slot and turn it
outcome: The coin's thin, flat, rigid edge fits into the screw's slot much like a screwdriver's blade does, since what the slot needs is a thin rigid tab, not a purpose-made tool, and turning it with enough grip loosens a screw that is not seated too tightly. On a screw that has rusted or is driven firmly, though, the coin's edge is softer and thinner than steel and starts to bend and round off under the twisting force before the screw gives, so after a few tries the coin is deformed enough that it no longer grips the slot at all, and the player is left with a still-stuck screw and a ruined coin.

numbers: how much force loosens it, how many turns to free it

latent: whether a thicker coin or a different edge would have held up better on this particular screw
state_after: coin: edge bent and rounded, no longer fits any slot well
screw: still partly stuck, loosened only slightly
chest lid: still closed
stress: a coin's incidental shape (thin, flat, rigid edge) doing a screwdriver's job right up to the point where a property it lacks (hardness comparable to steel) makes it fail and ruins the coin in the process
temptation: a rule 'coins work as screwdrivers' instead of deriving success from edge fit and turning force, and failure from copper's softness against a resistant screw
